newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-Africa braced for sharp rise in oil demand.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Africa braced for sharp rise in oil demand.

text.p: Africa, historically a petroleum producer rather than consumer, is emerging as one of the fastest growing demand centres for oil after years of stagnation, delegates at an oil conference heard this week.
Population growth and rapid urbanisation, coupled with new-found political stability south of the Sahara, has changed industry views on demand patterns, tempting new players into Africa.

"We believe Africa will be the next market, with a ready market in excess of 700 million people," said Dato' Hamzah Bakar of Malaysia's state oil company Petronas, which recently acquired 30 percent of South African Engen Ltd.
That 1.88 billion rand ($415 million) stake, the largest single foreign investment by Petronas to date, signalled its confidence in Africa, he told the Africa Oil meeting.

"With the exception of South Africa, the energy consumption (levels) of the African countries are still among the lowest in world which presents a tremendous growth opportunity for the oil and gas industry."

With African gross domestic growth (GDP) expected to average 4.9 percent for the next decade, demand for energy to fuel industrialisation and a growing transport sector will be paramount, he said. At the same time, growing economies will also boost demand for fertiliser and petrochemical feedstocks.
In South Africa, the continent's economic giant, oil demand is already hitting the buffers.
BP Africa managing director John Greensmith said the country could run out of gasoline refining capacity as early as this year and certainly by 1997, forcing imports of the product.
Overall South Africa oil consumption grew by 8.7 percent last year, far outstripping GDP growth of 3.3 percent.

Colin McClelland, director of the South African Petroleum Industry Association (Sapia), said gasoline supply and demand was now poised on a knife-edge -- although demand for middle distillates such as heating oil, diesel and kerosene would not outstrip national refining capacity until after 2000.
Latest Sapia figures show gasoline sales up five percent in the first half of 1996 against the same period last year, with even faster growth of 16 percent recorded for jet fuel.

In other areas, too, South Africa faces a looming shortage with ethylene demand expected to outstrip supply in around three years, according to Themis Themistocleous, oil and chemicals analyst at stockbroker SBC Warburg in Johannesburg.
Those shortfalls will require new capacity. But the oil industry has been wary of investing until the government clarifies plans for liberalising the oil market.
South Africa currently has three coastal oil refineries, two interior facilities owned or part-owned by synthetic fuel producer Sasol Ltd and a small fuel-from-gas plant.

Elsewhere in Africa there is a similar picture. Africa currently accounts for a meagre three percent of global petroleum consumption, but offtake is increasing sharply in several southern and eastern African countries.
Uganda, for example, saw demand increase over 10 percent last year and other countries had seen demand up by over five percent after years of negative growth, Greensmith said.
According to independent Houston-based consultant Antonio Szabo, Africa will need to invest $3.7 billion in new oil refining capacity to meet the expected growth in demand by 2020.

In many cases this will require a radical rethink of existing refineries in Africa, more than half of which are are too small ever to be viable and are costing the continent over $500 million a year in combined losses, according to World Bank oil and as division group leader Eric Daffern.
